title: The Straight Road and the Crooked
summary: Nothing is there, no nāda, no drop, no sun, no moon disc, and the king of mind is free by its own nature; the refrain warns against leaving the straight for the crooked, since awakening is near, and a bracelet on your own hand needs no mirror. What was ditch and gully to left and right has become the straight road, says Saraha. Munidatta reads the straight as the path of the avadhūtī, the central channel, and the far shore as the ultimate, where the best of yogins follow bodhicitta (cp.32.m3, cp.32.m5).

flags.note: Shastri prints dveśākha; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes de sha kha, which supports Deśākha, the glossary's form.

The poet's name is not in the heading line itself: the edition's attribution sarahapādānām, 'of Sarahapāda', stands at the head of 1a (removed there by emendation), and the Tibetan heading names sa ra ha'i zhabs. I moved it into the heading as '· Saraha'. Drop it if headings should carry only their own words.

lines.translit: nāda na bindu na rabi na śaśimaṇḍala
lines.gloss: nāda · not · drop · not · sun · not · moon disc

flags.note: bindu is rendered 'drop' as the glossary has it. Beside nāda it is the dot of the nasal written over a seed syllable, so 'dot' or the source form bindu might read better here.
The Tibetan has nyi zla'i dkyil 'khor, 'disc of sun and moon', taking 'disc' with both; the Bengali has rabi, 'sun', and śaśimaṇḍala, 'moon disc'. I follow the Bengali.

lines.en: The [king of mind]{king-of-mind} is free by its own [nature]{svabhava}.

flags.note: mukala is a past participle, 'freed, released' (Tibetan grol). 'Is free' rather than 'has been freed', since sahābe, 'by its own nature', suggests a standing state. Munidatta's paraphrase has cittaratna, 'jewel of mind', where the song has ciarāa, 'king of mind' (cp.32.m2).

lines.translit: uju re uju chāṛi mā lehu re baṅka
lines.gloss: straight · hey · straight · leaving · do not · take · hey · crooked
lines.en: Straight, hey! Don't leave the straight, hey, for the [crooked]{vakra}.

flags.note: The glossary files bare উজু under ujubata, 'straight road'. Here it is the adjective alone, twice, against baṅka, 'crooked'; 'straight road' would add a word the line lacks (the Tibetan adds lam, 'road'). I rendered it 'straight', left it unmarked, and listed it in termsOmitted. A variant 'straight' on ujubata would let it be linked.
re is a familiar vocative particle, rendered 'hey'; Munidatta calls it an address (cp.32.m3). The alternatives are 'O', or leaving it out.
The Tibetan line has gzhan, 'other', for baṅka, 'crooked', adds lam, 'road', and has no vocative.

lines.translit: niahi bohi mā jāhu re lāṅka
lines.gloss: near · awakening · do not · go · hey · Laṅkā (?)
lines.en: [Awakening]{bodhi} is near: don't go, hey, to [Laṅkā]{pl-lanka}.

flags.note: lāṅka has no glossary entry. I read it as Laṅkā, the far island of the Rāmāyaṇa and a byword for a distant place. The long first vowel matches kāṅkāṇa for kaṅkaṇa in 3a, and it rhymes with baṅka. The Tibetan has ring du, 'far' ('do not go far'), which fits that sense but may only translate it. Munidatta does not gloss the word. Alternatives: keep the source form lāṅka, or 'far'. I proposed an entry, pl-lanka.

niahi is taken as 'near', with the Tibetan nye'o and Munidatta's sannihita (cp.32.m3). nia can also be nija, 'own', as in niamaṇa (3b), and Munidatta calls awakening 'one's own city' (nijapura), so 'awakening is in yourself' is possible.
Shastri prints জাহুরে as one word; divided jāhu re, imperative 'go' plus the vocative re of 2a.

lines.gloss: on the hand · bracelet · do not · take · mirror
lines.en: For the [bracelet]{bracelet} on your hand, don't take a [mirror]{mirror}.

flags.note: hāthere is taken as the genitive hāthera with -e, 'on the hand', as Munidatta's citation hāthera and his hastasya, 'of the hand', suggest (cp.32.m4). It could also be divided hāthe re, 'on the hand, hey', with the vocative of the refrain.

lines.gloss: by oneself · self · let understand · own mind
lines.en: Let your own [mind]{citta} understand the [self]{atman} by itself.

flags.note: The Tibetan reads bdag gis bdag nyid nges par shes pas so, 'because by oneself one knows oneself with certainty': nges par, 'with certainty', where the Bengali has niamaṇa, 'own mind', as if reading Sanskrit niyamena. Its closing pas so also makes this line the reason for 3a. I follow the Bengali and Munidatta's nijamanasā (cp.32.m4).

bujhatu looks like a third-person imperative, 'let … understand', with niamaṇa as its subject. Munidatta has a second-person imperative with niamaṇa as the instrument: 'know with your own mind' (cp.32.m4). On his reading the line would be 'Understand the self by yourself, with your own mind.'

lines.gloss: far shore · on the near shore · that one · goes (?)
lines.en: On the far shore and the [near shore]{near-shore}, that one goes.

flags.note: gajii is uncertain. Munidatta's anugamyate, 'is followed, is gone along' (cp.32.m5), and the Tibetan 'gro ba, 'going', both read a verb of going, and I follow them. Prakrit gajjai would rather be 'roars' (Sanskrit garjati), and Bengali gajā- is 'sprout'; neither has support in the witnesses.

pāra is the noun 'far shore' here, paired with uāra, 'near shore'. The glossary's para is 'across', which suits the phrase pāra kar-, 'take across', but not this. I wrote 'far shore', unmarked, and listed it in termsOmitted.
soi is 'that one' or 'that very one'. The line does not say who; Munidatta supplies 'that very bodhicitta' (cp.32.m5).

lines.gloss: the wicked · with · going down · goes
lines.en: In the company of [the wicked]{durjana}, one goes down.

flags.note: abasari jāi is literally 'goes, having gone down or away' (compare Sanskrit ava-sṛ). 'Goes down' keeps both sinking, as in Munidatta's majjanti, 'they sink' (cp.32.m5), and coming to ruin. The glossary suggests 'goes to ruin'; the Tibetan has 'dies'.
The Tibetan has sdug pa'i skye bo, perhaps a slip for gdug pa'i, 'harmful', the word of its comment, and 'chi bar 'gyur, 'comes to die', for abasari jāi.
The companion entry is detected in সাঙ্গে, which here is the postposition 'with, in the company of'. Omitted; see termsOmitted.

lines.en: [Left and right]{vama-daksina}, what was ditch and gully—

flags.note: khāla is a ditch or channel (Bengali khāl). bikhalā is uncertain: perhaps an echo-word extending khāla ('ditches and the like'), perhaps from vi- with skhal-, 'slip'. The Tibetan has dong dang g.yang, 'pit and precipice'. 'Gully' is a stopgap.

There is no verb in this line. I take the relative jo with bhāilā in 5b: 'what was ditch and gully … has become the straight road'; 'was' is supplied from that past tense. The Tibetan takes jo as 'whose' (gang gi): the road with pit and precipice right and left is itself the straight road. That reading would give 'Where left and right are ditch and gully, / … that is the straight road.'

lines.gloss: Saraha · says · father · straight road · became
lines.en: [Saraha]{p-saraha} says, [father]{father}, it has become the [straight road]{ujubata}.

flags.note: bapā is filed under father, and I kept 'father'. It looks like an affectionate address, as Bengali bābā and bāpu are still said to a son or a younger person, and the Tibetan has the vocative kye, 'O', in its place. 'My dear' or 'my son' would give the tone; 'father' keeps the word.

In Toh 2293 Munidatta's introduction to the song follows this line without a break (… drang po'i lam mo kye/ de kho na nyid kyi don …). It is treated as the introduction segment cp.32.m1, not part of 5b.

notes.text: Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Each song's heading names the rāga it is sung to; this one is Deśākha.

Shastri prints dveśākha. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heads the song de sha kha zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs sa ra ha'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the melody called de sha kha, of Sarahapāda', which supports the spelling Deśākha. The edition's attribution, sarahapādānām, 'of Sarahapāda', stands before the first line; the draft moves the poet's name into the heading.

Munidatta introduces the song: the siddha master Sarahapāda, through realizing all dharmas, sets out that same meaning for the sake of people. The Tibetan comment has 'the meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid kyi don).

Nāda, 'sound, resonance': in mantra meditation, the subtle sound into which a seed syllable is said to dissolve, written as a fine stroke above the bindu, the dot of the nasal; 'drop' renders bindu. In tantric visualization a sun disc and a moon disc serve as seats on which a syllable or deity arises. The line says none of the four is there.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads nA da thig le nyi zla'i dkyil 'khor med, 'no nāda, drop, or disc of sun and moon'. It keeps nāda in transcription and takes 'disc' with both sun and moon, where the Bengali has rabi, 'sun', and śaśimaṇḍala, 'moon disc'.

Ciarāa is Sanskrit cittarāja, 'king of mind', the mind spoken of as a king; the Tibetan line has sems kyi rgyal po. Sahābe is svabhāvena, 'by its own nature', and mukala is 'freed' (Tibetan grol). Munidatta's paraphrase has cittaratna, 'jewel of mind', in place of the king, and the Tibetan comment sems kyi rin po che.

Munidatta: by the power of the waves of nectar from the true guru's mouth, the jewel of mind of those who know the ultimate is freed by its own nature, because the concepts of nāda, bindu and the rest are abandoned; those whose sight is filmed over by beginningless ignorance see things otherwise. He then cites a verse of Saraha by its opening words only (aho gaṭa…).
The refrain sets the straight against the crooked, as of roads; the last line names the straight road (ujubāṭa) outright. Re, three times, is a familiar call to the listener, like 'hey'.

Munidatta calls the refrain praise of the path. Apart from the path of the avadhūtī the lord of yogis has no other means; going by it, awakening, one's own city, is very near. Re is an address: 'O novice yogin, do not resort to the crooked path; do not become a wanderer in saṃsāra again.' The Tibetan comment has 'the king's palace' (rgyal po'i pho brang) for 'one's own city'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads drang po'i lam spangs gzhan ni ma len cig, 'abandoning the straight road, do not take another'. It adds lam, 'road', has gzhan, 'other', for baṅka, 'crooked', and has no vocative. Its comment has lam kyog po, 'crooked path'.

Lāṅka is read here as Laṅkā, Rāvaṇa's island beyond the southern sea in the Rāmāyaṇa, a byword for a far place; the long first vowel matches kāṅkāṇa for kaṅkaṇa in 3a. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has ring du, 'far', in its place (byang chub nye'o ring du ma 'gro re, 'awakening is near; do not go far'), which fits that sense. Munidatta does not take up the word.

Niahi is taken as 'near', with the Tibetan nye'o, 'is near', and Munidatta's sannihita, 'near at hand'. Nia can also be nija, 'own', as in niamaṇa, 'own mind' (3b), and Munidatta's paraphrase calls awakening 'one's own city' (nijapura), so 'awakening is in yourself' is a possible reading. Shastri prints jāhure as one word; it is divided jāhu re, 'go, hey'.
A bracelet on one's own hand is in plain sight, so a mirror to look at it is needless. The line has the ring of a proverb; the second line of the couplet turns from it to knowing the self by oneself.
The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads lag gdub lta la me long ma len cig, 'do not take a mirror to look at the bracelet', adding 'to look'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads bdag gis bdag nyid nges par shes pas so, 'because by oneself one knows oneself with certainty'. Where the Bengali has niamaṇa, 'own mind', it has nges par, 'with certainty', as if reading Sanskrit niyamena, and its closing pas so makes the line the reason for 3a. Munidatta reads nijamanasā, 'with your own mind', which the draft follows.

Munidatta calls this couplet, his 'second verse', a statement of self-conviction. What will you do with a mirror for the bracelet on your hand? 'O novice yogin, by the vajra guru's grace know with your own mind the true nature of bodhicitta'; by that you will directly realize the unsurpassed Dharma. He puts bodhicitta where the song has the self (apā).
Pāra and uāra are the far and the near bank of a river, the two ends of a crossing. Who 'that one' (soi) is, the line does not say.

Gajii is uncertain. Munidatta paraphrases with anugamyate, 'is followed, is gone along', and the Tibetan line has 'gro ba, 'going': both read a verb of going, which the draft follows. Prakrit gajjai would rather mean 'roars' (Sanskrit garjati), and Bengali gajā- means 'sprout'; neither has support in the witnesses. Munidatta cites the two shores as one word, pāroāre.

Munidatta calls the couplet, his 'third verse', praise of bodhicitta. On the far shore, 'by the ultimate', that very bodhicitta is followed by the best of yogins, who then attain the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā by the guru's grace. On the near shore (his citation of the word is corrupt, deāra?) it is followed in existence by ordinary people, who, keeping company with the wicked, delusion and the rest, sink in the ocean of saṃsāra.

Abasari jāi is literally 'goes, having gone down or away' (compare Sanskrit ava-sṛ). 'Goes down' keeps both senses open: sinking, as in Munidatta's majjanti, 'they sink', and coming to ruin. Sāṅge is the postposition 'with, in the company of'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads sdug pa'i skye bo dang 'grogs 'chi bar 'gyur, 'keeping company with sdug pa'i people, one comes to die': 'dies' where the Bengali has abasari jāi. Sdug pa'i is perhaps a slip for gdug pa'i, 'harmful', the word of the Tibetan comment (gti mug la sogs pa gdug pa'i skye bo).

Khāla is a ditch or channel (compare Bengali khāl, 'canal, creek'). Bikhalā is uncertain: perhaps an echo-word extending khāla, 'ditches and the like', perhaps vi- with khal-, 'slip, stumble' (Sanskrit skhal-). The Tibetan line has dong dang g.yang, 'pit and precipice'. 'Gully' is a stopgap.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads gang gi g.yas g.yon dag ni dong dang g.yang / sa ra has smras drang po'i lam mo kye, 'that whose right and left are pit and precipice: Saraha said, it is the straight road, O!' It takes jo as 'whose', so that a road with a drop on either side is itself the straight road. The draft takes jo with bhāilā: what was ditch and gully has become the straight road.

Bapā is literally 'father' (compare Bengali bāp), apparently used as an affectionate address, as Bengali bābā and bāpu are still said to a son or a younger person. The Tibetan line has the vocative particle kye, 'O', in its place. Saraha names himself here, as the poets do in the last couplet.

Munidatta calls this couplet, his 'fourth verse', praise of the path again; he says it is easy to understand and leaves the left and right unexplained. He adds Saraha's words: for going to the city of great bliss, the path of the avadhūtī is excellent and not crooked. He then quotes 'another caryā', apparently a version of the last couplet of song 15: with no toll station or guard post, walk the road with eyes closed (the Tibetan has 'the road seen by the eye').
In the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) Munidatta's introduction to the song (de kho na nyid kyi don…) follows this line without a break. It belongs to the commentary (cp.32.m1), not to the verse.

termsOmitted.reason: Bare উজু is the adjective 'straight' (twice), not the compound ujubāṭa. The glossary's 'straight road' would add 'road', which the Bengali line lacks (the Tibetan adds lam). Rendered 'straight', unmarked; the reviewer is asked whether to add 'straight' as a variant of ujubata.

Here pāra is the noun 'far shore', paired with uāra, 'near shore'. The glossary's 'across' renders the phrase pāra kar-, 'take across', and does not fit. Rendered 'far shore', unmarked; the reviewer is asked whether to add a variant.
সাঙ্গে here is the postposition 'with, in the company of' (dujjaṇa sāṅge, 'with the wicked'), not the noun 'companion'; rendered 'in the company of'.

proposals.definition: Laṅkā: in the Rāmāyaṇa, Rāvaṇa's island city beyond the southern sea, usually identified with Sri Lanka, and so a byword for a distant place. Song 32 (2b) seems to name it as where one need not go, since awakening is near; the Tibetan line has ring du, 'far'. Reading lāṅka as Laṅkā is tentative.
proposals.rationale: The refrain's lāṅka has no entry. Reading it as Laṅkā keeps a concrete place where the Tibetan gives only the sense 'far'; the long first vowel matches kāṅkāṇa for kaṅkaṇa in 3a, and the word rhymes with baṅka. Munidatta does not gloss it. The Tibetan form is recorded as a sense rendering, not as a match. If the reviewer prefers the source form or 'far', drop or recast this entry.

questions: 2a: the glossary files bare উজু under ujubata ('straight road'). I rendered it 'straight', unmarked, and listed it in termsOmitted, because 'straight road' adds a word the line lacks (the Tibetan adds lam). Should 'straight' become a variant of ujubata so the refrain can be linked, or would you rather have 'straight road' here?
2b: lāṅka has no entry. I read it as Laṅkā, a byword for a far place, and proposed pl-lanka (keep-source). Accept this, keep the source form lāṅka, or render 'far' with the Tibetan ring du?

5b: বপা is filed under father, and I kept 'father'. It looks like an affectionate address (the Tibetan has kye, 'O'). Would you prefer 'my dear' or 'my son', or a separate entry for the address? The father entry's definition currently describes only the father of song 20.
4a: the glossary's para is 'across', which suits pāra kar- but not the noun 'far shore' paired with uāra here. I wrote 'far shore', unmarked. Add 'far shore' as a variant, or a separate noun entry?
2a, 2b: I used 'hey' for the vocative re (three times). Would you prefer 'O', or leaving it out?
1a: is bindu as 'drop' right beside nāda, or would 'dot' or the source form bindu serve better here?

3b: I took niamaṇa as the subject of bujhatu ('Let your own mind understand the self by itself'). Munidatta reads it as the instrument ('know … with your own mind'), and the Tibetan as nges par, 'with certainty'. Is the subject reading acceptable?

5a–5b: I read 'what was ditch and gully has become the straight road', supplying 'was' from bhāilā. The Tibetan reads 'that whose right and left are pit and precipice is the straight road'. Which should the English follow? And is 'gully' acceptable for the uncertain bikhalā?
4a: gajii as 'goes', with Munidatta's anugamyate and the Tibetan 'gro ba; and 4b abasari jāi as 'goes down'. Agree?
Heading: I moved '· Saraha' into the heading from the attribution sarahapādānām, which the edition prints before 1a. Keep it?
4b: the companion entry is detected in সাঙ্গে, which here only means 'with'. Should its match be narrowed so the postposition is not counted?
